questions.q: In the nineteenth century, physical sciences were divided into how many distinct disciplines?
questions.explanation: Physics, chemistry, astronomy, geology and meteorology — five disciplines, of which physics is the most fundamental.

questions.q: Which is the most fundamental of all the physical sciences?
questions.explanation: Other sciences rely on the principles of physics, so physics is called the most fundamental science.

questions.q: Biology uses the physics principle of ______ to understand how blood flows through the heart, arteries and veins.
questions.explanation: Blood flow is explained by the physics of fluid movement.

questions.q: Which branch of physics deals with heat and its transformation into other forms of energy?
questions.explanation: Thermodynamics is the study of heat, temperature and energy transfer.

questions.q: Physical quantities are those quantities which:
questions.explanation: A physical quantity can be measured and is expressed as a number with a unit.

questions.q: Which of the following is a non-physical quantity?
questions.explanation: Taste, feeling and colour cannot be measured, so they are non-physical quantities.

questions.q: Measurement is a comparison of an unknown quantity with a known:
questions.explanation: Measurement compares an unknown physical quantity with a standard to see how large or small it is.

questions.q: In the statement "the length of a person is 1.65 m", the number 1.65 is called the:
questions.explanation: A measurement = numerical magnitude (1.65) × unit (metre).

questions.q: Which of the following is a base physical quantity?
questions.explanation: Mass is one of the seven base quantities; velocity, area and force are derived from base quantities.

questions.q: Physical quantities obtained by multiplying or dividing base quantities are called:
questions.explanation: Derived quantities (area, speed, force, etc.) are formed from base quantities.

questions.q: Which of the following is a derived quantity?
questions.explanation: Density = mass ÷ volume, so it is derived from mass and length.

questions.q: The cubit, used by the Egyptians to build the pyramids, is the length from the:
options: elbow to the tip of the middle finger
questions.explanation: A cubit is the measure from the elbow to the tip of the middle finger with the arm extended.

questions.q: How many base quantities are chosen in the International System of Units (SI)?
questions.explanation: SI has seven base quantities: length, mass, time, electric current, temperature, amount of substance and light intensity.

questions.q: SI is the short form of the French name "Système International d'Unités", which means:
questions.explanation: SI stands for the International System of Units.

questions.q: The SI unit of electric current is:
questions.explanation: Ampere (A) is the SI base unit of electric current.

questions.q: The SI unit of temperature is:
questions.explanation: Kelvin (K) is the SI base unit of temperature.

questions.q: The SI base unit of light (luminous) intensity is:
questions.explanation: Candela (cd) is the base unit of light intensity.

questions.q: The symbol of the SI unit of amount of substance is:
questions.explanation: The mole is written as 'mol'.

questions.q: The SI unit of acceleration is:
questions.explanation: Acceleration = change in velocity ÷ time, so its unit is m s⁻².

questions.q: One newton (N) in terms of base units is:
questions.explanation: F = ma, so N = kg × m s⁻² = kg m s⁻².

questions.q: One pascal (Pa) in terms of base units is:
questions.explanation: Pressure = force ÷ area = kg m s⁻² ÷ m² = kg m⁻¹ s⁻².

questions.q: One joule (J) in terms of base units is:
questions.explanation: Energy = force × distance = kg m s⁻² × m = kg m² s⁻².

questions.q: The SI unit of density is:
questions.explanation: Density = mass ÷ volume, so the unit is kg m⁻³.

questions.q: Which of the following is NOT an SI base unit?
questions.explanation: Newton is a derived unit (kg m s⁻²); metre, second and kelvin are base units.

questions.q: In scientific notation (standard form), the mantissa must be:
options: equal to or greater than 1 and less than 10
questions.explanation: Number = mantissa × 10ⁿ, where 1 ≤ mantissa < 10.

questions.q: 0.00045 m written in scientific notation is:
questions.explanation: Moving the decimal 4 places right gives 4.5, so the exponent is −4.

questions.q: The mass of the Earth, 5,980,000,000,000,000,000,000,000 kg, in scientific notation is:
questions.explanation: The decimal moves 24 places to the left, so the power of ten is 24.

questions.q: The number of seconds in a day (86 400 s) in standard form is:
questions.explanation: 86 400 = 8.64 × 10⁴ (decimal moved 4 places left).

questions.q: The prefix "mega" represents:
questions.explanation: Mega (M) = 10⁶.

questions.q: The prefix "nano" represents:
questions.explanation: Nano (n) = 10⁻⁹.

questions.q: The diameter of a proton, 1.7 × 10⁻¹⁵ m, can be written as:
questions.explanation: 10⁻¹⁵ = femto (f), so 1.7 × 10⁻¹⁵ m = 1.7 fm.

questions.q: 86.4 ks is equal to:
Which of the following prefixes represents the smallest value?
questions.explanation: pico = 10⁻¹² is smaller than nano (10⁻⁹), micro (10⁻⁶) and milli (10⁻³).

questions.q: 1 µm is equal to:
questions.explanation: micro (µ) = 10⁻⁶.

questions.q: 5000 g can be written with a prefix as:
The thickness of a sheet of paper, 100 000 nm, in metres is:
Pakistan's power capacity of 40 000 MW is equal to:
A scalar quantity is completely described by its:
questions.explanation: Scalars need only magnitude (size) with a unit, e.g. 30 s.

questions.q: Which of the following is a vector quantity?
questions.explanation: Displacement needs both magnitude and direction.

questions.q: Which of the following is a scalar quantity?
questions.explanation: Temperature has magnitude only; weight, momentum and acceleration have direction.

questions.q: Which of the following is a vector quantity?
questions.explanation: Electric field strength acts in a definite direction, so it is a vector.

questions.q: Weight is a vector quantity because:
options: it always acts towards the centre of the Earth
it changes from place to place
it is a type of energy
questions.explanation: Weight is a force with a definite direction (towards the Earth's centre).

questions.q: You take 5 s to reach the classroom door and 20 s more to reach the school gate, so the total time is 25 s. This shows that time:
options: is a scalar added by ordinary algebra
questions.explanation: Scalars are added, subtracted and multiplied by the ordinary rules of algebra.

questions.q: Graphically, a vector is represented by:
options: a line segment with an arrow head
questions.explanation: The length of the arrow (to scale) gives magnitude and the arrow head gives direction.

questions.q: In the head-to-tail rule, the resultant vector is drawn from the:
options: head of the first vector to the tail of the last
tail of the first vector to the head of the last
tail of the last vector to the head of the first
questions.explanation: Joining the tail of the first vector to the head of the last gives the resultant.

questions.q: Two forces of 3 N and 4 N act at right angles to each other. The magnitude of their resultant is:
questions.explanation: R = √(3² + 4²) = √25 = 5 N (Pythagoras theorem).

questions.q: A boy walks 6 m east and then 8 m north. The magnitude of his displacement is:
questions.explanation: Displacement = √(6² + 8²) = √100 = 10 m.

questions.q: If vector A lies along the x-axis and vector B along the y-axis, the direction of their resultant from the x-axis is θ =
questions.explanation: tan θ = perpendicular/base = B/A, so θ = tan⁻¹(B/A).

questions.q: The point where the x-axis and y-axis of a coordinate system intersect is called the:
questions.explanation: The point of intersection of the two axes is the origin O.

questions.q: The least count of a metre rule is:
questions.explanation: A metre rule has 1000 small divisions of 1 mm each.

questions.q: The minimum value that can be measured on the scale of an instrument is called its:
questions.explanation: The measurement of every instrument is limited to its least count.

questions.q: The least count of vernier callipers is found by:
options: smallest main scale division ÷ total number of vernier scale divisions
questions.explanation: Least count = smallest division on main scale ÷ total divisions on vernier scale.

questions.q: If the smallest main scale division is 1 mm and the vernier scale has 10 divisions, the least count is:
If the smallest main scale division is 1 mm and the vernier scale has 20 divisions, the least count is:
The internal diameter of a beaker is measured with the ______ of vernier callipers.
questions.explanation: Inside jaws are used for internal diameters of hollow objects.

questions.q: Which part of vernier callipers is used to measure the depth of a small hole?
questions.explanation: The depth probe slides into a hole to measure its depth.

questions.q: When the jaws are closed, the zero of the vernier scale is to the RIGHT of the zero of the main scale. The zero error is:
questions.explanation: Vernier zero to the right of main scale zero gives a positive zero error.

questions.q: When the jaws are closed, the zero of the vernier scale is to the LEFT of the zero of the main scale. The zero error is:
questions.explanation: Vernier zero to the left of main scale zero gives a negative zero error.

questions.q: Main scale reading is 2.3 cm and the 6th vernier division coincides. If the least count is 0.01 cm, the total reading is:
The least count of digital vernier callipers is:
questions.explanation: Digital vernier callipers have a least count of 0.01 mm, so they are more precise.

questions.q: A measuring tape is most suitable for measuring:
options: the depth of a test tube
questions.explanation: A measuring tape is a flexible ruler for larger distances, typically a few metres.

questions.q: A screw gauge is used for measuring lengths even smaller than those measured by:
questions.explanation: A screw gauge (least count 0.01 mm) is more precise than vernier callipers (0.1 mm).

questions.q: The distance travelled by the circular scale on the main (linear) scale in one complete rotation is called:
questions.explanation: This distance is the pitch of the screw gauge.

questions.q: The least count of a screw gauge is equal to:
options: pitch ÷ total number of divisions on circular scale
questions.explanation: Least count = pitch ÷ total divisions on the circular scale.

questions.q: A screw gauge has a pitch of 0.5 mm and 50 divisions on its circular scale. Its least count is:
A screw gauge has a pitch of 1 mm and 100 circular scale divisions. Its least count is:
The least count of a screw gauge in centimetres is:
The ratchet of a screw gauge is used to:
options: prevent too much pressure on the object
questions.explanation: Turning the ratchet until it clicks stops the user from over-tightening the object.

questions.q: Main scale reading is 3.5 mm and the 28th circular division is in line with the datum line. With least count 0.01 mm, the reading is:
Which instrument is best to measure the diameter of a thin wire?
questions.explanation: The screw gauge has the smallest least count, so it gives the most precise reading for thin wires.

questions.q: When the spindle touches the anvil, the zero of the circular scale has NOT reached the datum line. The zero error is:
questions.explanation: According to the book, the zero error is positive if the circular scale zero has not reached the main scale zero.

questions.q: A screw gauge is also called a:
questions.explanation: It is also known as a micrometer screw gauge.

quizzes.topic: Mass, Volume and Time Measurement & Estimation

questions.q: The first mass-measuring instrument invented was the:
questions.explanation: The balance (beam balance) was the first mass-measuring instrument.

questions.q: A physical balance is so sensitive that it can measure masses of the order of:
questions.explanation: A physical balance can measure mass in the milligram range.

questions.q: A physical balance is placed in a glass case so that:
options: dust and wind cannot affect its accuracy
questions.explanation: The protective glass case keeps out dust and air currents.

questions.q: The levelling screws of a physical balance are used to:
options: find the zero error of the pointer scale
questions.explanation: Levelling screws make the balance horizontal before use.

questions.q: A measuring cylinder is used to measure the:
questions.explanation: A measuring (graduated) cylinder measures the volume of liquids.

questions.q: The scale of a measuring cylinder is usually marked in:
questions.explanation: Volume is read in millilitres (mL) or cubic centimetres (cm³).

questions.q: The water level in a measuring cylinder rises from 40 cm³ to 55 cm³ when a stone is completely immersed. The volume of the stone is:
questions.explanation: Volume of stone = final reading − initial reading = 55 − 40 = 15 cm³.

questions.q: While reading a measuring cylinder, the eye should be:
options: level with the bottom of the meniscus
questions.explanation: Reading at eye level with the bottom of the meniscus avoids parallax error.

questions.q: The duration of a specific interval of time is measured by a:
questions.explanation: A stopwatch measures time intervals.

questions.q: According to the book, the least count of a digital stopwatch is generally:
questions.explanation: The book states: analogue stopwatch least count 1 s, digital stopwatch 0.1 s.

questions.q: The right button of a digital stopwatch is used to:
options: reset it and record lap (split) times
questions.explanation: The left button starts/stops; the right button resets and records lap times.

questions.q: A reasonable estimate of the height of a classroom door is about:
questions.explanation: A door is a little taller than an adult, about 2 m.

questions.q: A reasonable estimate of the mass of a grade 9 student is about:
questions.explanation: A teenager typically has a mass of around 40–60 kg.

questions.q: The uncertainty that arises during a measurement is called:
questions.explanation: Every measurement has some doubt, called error.

questions.q: Errors that occur consistently in one direction (always positive or always negative) are called:
questions.explanation: Systematic errors shift all readings in the same direction.

questions.q: Zero error of an instrument is an example of:
questions.explanation: Instrumental errors, including zero errors, are systematic errors.

questions.q: Random errors can be reduced by:
options: taking repeated readings and finding their mean
questions.explanation: Random errors are unpredictable, so averaging many readings reduces their effect.

questions.q: Systematic errors can be reduced by:
options: improving technique, choosing better instruments and correcting zero error
questions.explanation: Better instruments and techniques remove the cause of systematic error.

questions.q: An error caused by an observer's bias or carelessness is a:
questions.explanation: Personal errors arise from bias, improper setup or carelessness.

questions.q: The time for 10 oscillations of a simple pendulum is 20.0 s. The period (time for one oscillation) is:
questions.explanation: Period = total time ÷ number of oscillations = 20.0 ÷ 10 = 2.0 s.

questions.q: We time 10 oscillations instead of one mainly to reduce error due to:
questions.explanation: Human reflexes are slow; timing many oscillations reduces the effect of reaction time.

questions.q: Three readings of a length are 2.31 cm, 2.33 cm and 2.32 cm. The average value is:
Precision is the degree of:
options: closeness of a measured value to the true value
agreement between repeated measurements of the same quantity
size of the least count only
questions.explanation: Precision means consistency and repeatability of results.

questions.q: Accuracy refers to how close a measured value is to the:
questions.explanation: Accuracy is closeness to the true value.

questions.q: A thermometer always reads 2 °C higher than the actual temperature. Its readings are:
questions.explanation: Readings are consistent (precise) but always away from the true value (not accurate).

questions.q: Darts land near the centre of the target but are scattered all over. The throws are:
questions.explanation: Close to the bullseye = accurate; scattered = not precise.

questions.q: Significant figures are:
options: all accurately known digits and the first doubtful digit
only the digits after the decimal
questions.explanation: Accurately known digits + first doubtful digit = significant figures.

questions.q: The number of significant figures in 23.457 is:
questions.explanation: All non-zero digits are significant: 2, 3, 4, 5, 7.

questions.q: The number of significant figures in 0.0029 is:
questions.explanation: Leading zeros are only place holders; only 2 and 9 are significant.

questions.q: The number of significant figures in 0.00290 is:
questions.explanation: The final zero after a non-zero digit is significant: 2, 9, 0.

questions.q: The number of significant figures in 100.8 s is:
questions.explanation: Zeros between significant digits are significant: 1, 0, 0, 8.

questions.q: The number of significant figures in 210.0 g is:
questions.explanation: The zero after the decimal point and the zero between 1 and the decimal are significant.

questions.q: How many significant figures are shown in 2.900 × 10⁴?
questions.explanation: In scientific notation all digits of the mantissa (2, 9, 0, 0) are significant.

questions.q: "29,000 spectators watched a match" is an estimate. The number of significant figures is:
questions.explanation: Only 2 and 9 are measured; the zeros just show place value.

questions.q: 3.876 rounded off to two decimal places is:
questions.explanation: The dropped digit 6 ≥ 5, so 7 becomes 8 → 3.88.

questions.q: 657.873 rounded off to two decimal places is:
questions.explanation: The dropped digit 3 < 5, so 7 stays the same → 657.87.

questions.q: 24.68 rounded off to three significant figures is:
questions.explanation: Dropping 8 (≥ 5) increases 6 to 7 → 24.7.

questions.q: 7,847 rounded off to three significant figures is:
questions.explanation: The last digit 7 is replaced by zero and, being ≥ 5, raises 4 to 5 → 7,850.

questions.q: 0.07683 rounded off to three significant figures is:
questions.explanation: Dropping 3 (< 5) leaves 0.0768.

questions.q: Which one of the following units is not a derived unit?
questions.explanation: Kilogram is an SI base unit; pascal, newton and watt are derived.

questions.q: Amount of a substance in terms of numbers is measured in:
questions.explanation: The mole is the SI base unit of amount of substance.

questions.q: The number of significant figures in 0.00650 s is:
questions.explanation: Leading zeros are not significant; 6, 5 and the final 0 are.

questions.q: Which of the following numbers shows 4 significant digits?
Which of the following prefixes represents the largest value?
questions.explanation: peta = 10¹⁵ is larger than mega (10⁶) and kilo (10³).

questions.q: A micrometer can be used to measure:
questions.explanation: A micrometer (screw gauge) measures small lengths.

questions.q: The instrument that best measures the internal diameter of a pipe is:
questions.explanation: Vernier callipers have inside jaws for internal diameters.

questions.q: The least count of a screw gauge is 0.01 mm. If the main scale reading is zero and the third line of its circular scale coincides with the datum line, the measurement is:
questions.explanation: Reading = 0 + 3 × 0.01 mm = 0.03 mm.

questions.q: 9.483 × 10³ m is the standard form of:
Which of the following is a base unit?
questions.explanation: Mole is one of the seven SI base units.

questions.q: The number having one significant digit is:
questions.explanation: In 6 × 10² only the digit 6 is significant; the others have two.

questions.q: The ratio of millimetre to micrometre is:
questions.explanation: 10⁻³ m ÷ 10⁻⁶ m = 10³ = 1000 (a ratio has no unit).

questions.q: 0.2 mm in metres is:
